summary: Target-level plan of rigid-analytic Zariski geometry, extending AdicSpacesPartII. RZ.0 defines Zariski closed subsets and local dimension, supplies regularity of affinoid restriction, proves Conrad's criteria for nowhere density and that images of proper morphisms are Zariski closed. RZ.1 constructs the normalization of a rigid space, its connected and irreducible components (Conrad §§1.2, 2.1–2.2), the irreducibility criterion (Lemma 2.2.3), the full-dimension criterion (Corollary 2.2.7) and the connectedness of dense Zariski opens of irreducible spaces. RZ.2 defines the singular locus, identifies smooth and regular loci in characteristic 0, and proves the finite stratification of a reduced finite-dimensional space by smooth strata and the Zariski openness of maximal-rank loci of differentials. RZ.3 treats classical points, their density, rigid analytic points of diamonds (Howe–Klevdal Definition 2.2.1(1), Remark 2.2.2), the L-points of polydiscs and the Gauss point in the closure of the rational points when the residue field is infinite. RZ.4 is Bhatt–Hansen §2.1: specialisation, Shilov and weakly Shilov points, Abhyankar's bound and the transcendence criterion, and Corollary 2.10. RZ.5 is Temkin's functorial resolution: blow-up sequences, the scheme-level theorems (proposed for transfer to an AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry Part II), Theorems 5.2.2/5.3.2 for rigid spaces and the consequences Howe–Klevdal use. RZ.6 gives analytic manifolds of rational points of smooth rigid spaces, the analytic inverse function theorem, polydisc neighbourhoods, the constant rank theorem in characteristic 0, submersions from smooth morphisms, and the identity theorem across a closed subfield.

nodes.title: Zariski closed subsets of a rigid space
nodes.statement: Let K be a complete nonarchimedean field with a nontrivial rank-one absolute value and X a rigid space over K (an adic space locally of finite type over Spa(K, K°)). A subset Z ⊆ |X| is Zariski closed if Z = Supp(O_X/𝓘) = {x ∈ |X| : 𝓘_x ≠ O_{X,x}} for a coherent ideal 𝓘 ⊆ O_X (AdicSpacesPartII:R3/coherent-ideal-closed-subspace); equivalently Z is the underlying set of a closed adic subspace. On an affinoid open U = Spa(A, A°) ⊆ X with 𝓘|_U = Ĩ for an ideal I ⊆ A, Z ∩ U = V(I) = {x ∈ U : |f(x)| = 0 for all f ∈ I}. The reduced structure on Z is the closed adic subspace Z_red defined by the largest coherent ideal with support Z, which on U is √I; Zariski closed subsets correspond bijectively to radical coherent ideals. A Zariski open subset is the complement of a Zariski closed subset. The Zariski closed subsets of X are the closed sets of a topology on |X| coarser than its own topology.
hypotheses: X is locally noetherian, so coherent ideals and their radicals are coherent and every affinoid open has a strongly noetherian Tate coordinate ring.

On a quasi-separated X, Huber's functor (AdicSpacesPartII:R1/rigid-adic-comparison-functor) carries Tate's analytic subsets (zero loci of coherent ideals on the classical rigid space) to Zariski closed subsets, and the classical points of V(I) are the maximal ideals of A containing I.
proofSteps: The support of the coherent sheaf O_X/𝓘 is closed, and on U it is V(I) because (O_X/𝓘)_x = 0 iff some f ∈ I is a unit at x iff |f(x)| ≠ 0 for some f ∈ I.

For I ⊆ A, radical formation commutes with affinoid restriction because the quotient by √I is reduced and remains reduced on rational domains (AdicSpacesPartII:R5/reduced-affinoid-rational-localisation), and arbitrary affinoid restrictions are covered by rational domains. Flatness preserves the exact quotient sequence; reducedness, rather than flatness alone, identifies its nilradical. The resulting radical ideals glue coherently.
Unions and intersections: V(𝓘) ∪ V(𝓙) = V(𝓘𝓙) and ∩_α V(𝓘_α) = V(Σ_α 𝓘_α), the sum being coherent locally because A is noetherian; hence a topology.
Preimages: for f : Y → X, f^{-1}(V(𝓘)) = V(𝓘·O_Y).
acceptance: On the closed unit disc D = Spa(K⟨T⟩, K°⟨T⟩), V(T) is the single classical point T = 0, and the Gauss point does not lie on any proper Zariski closed subset.
On Spa(K⟨T⟩/(T²)), V(T) is all of |X|: Zariski closed subsets see only the reduction.

nodes.title: Local dimension of a rigid space at a point
nodes.statement: For X a rigid space over K and x ∈ |X|, the local dimension is dim_x X = min{dim O_X(U) : U ∋ x an affinoid open}, where dim O_X(U) is the Krull dimension of the K-affinoid algebra O_X(U) (−∞ for the empty space). The dimension of X is dim X = sup_{x} dim_x X. For a Zariski closed Z ⊆ X and z ∈ Z, dim_z Z means the local dimension of Z_red at z.
hypotheses: The minimum exists because the Krull dimension of a nonzero K-affinoid algebra is a natural number (Noether normalization, AdicSpacesPartII:R0/affinoid-noether-normalisation).
At a classical point, dim_x X equals dim O_{X,x}; prove this using the minimal primes of one affinoid ring and the equidimensionality of affinoid domains, without using global irreducible components.
proofSteps: If U′ ⊆ U are affinoid neighbourhoods of x then dim O(U′) ≤ dim O(U): an affinoid subdomain inclusion is flat with the same completed local rings at classical points (AdicSpacesPartII:R1/rigid-local-ring-completion), and the Krull dimension of an affinoid algebra is the maximum of the dimensions of its local rings at maximal ideals (Jacobson, AdicSpacesPartII:R0/affinoid-jacobson).

Hence dim_x X is computed on arbitrarily small affinoid neighbourhoods, x ↦ dim_x X is upper semicontinuous, and dim_x Y ≤ dim_x X for a locally closed immersion Y ↪ X (a closed subspace of an affinoid has smaller Krull dimension; open immersions do not change local dimension).

On U = Spa(A), write its finitely many minimal primes as p_i. Remove the closed union V(p_i) for those not contained in the maximal ideal m_x. Each remaining A/p_i is an affinoid domain, whose maximal localizations have dimension dim(A/p_i). Restrict to a small affinoid neighbourhood inside this complement. The maximum of these dimensions is both dim_x X and dim A_m; completion identifies the latter with dim O_{X,x}.
acceptance: The closed unit polydisc of dimension n has local dimension n at every point, the Gauss point included.
Spa(K⟨T⟩ × K) has local dimension 1 at the points of the disc and 0 at the isolated classical point.

nodes.title: Criteria for a Zariski closed subset to be nowhere dense
nodes.statement: Let X be a rigid space over K and Z ⊆ X a Zariski closed subset. The following are equivalent: (a) Z contains no nonempty open subset of |X|; (b) Z contains no nonempty affinoid open subset of X; (c) for every affinoid open Spa(A, A°) ⊆ X with Z ∩ Spa(A, A°) = V(I), the ideal I lies in no minimal prime of A (equivalently Spec(A/I) is nowhere dense in Spec A); (d) dim O_{Z,z} < dim O_{X,z} for every classical point z ∈ Z; (e) dim_z Z < dim_z X for every z ∈ Z. Such Z is called nowhere dense. The condition is local on X and depends only on X_red and Z_red.
hypotheses: X is a rigid space over K (locally noetherian); Z carries its reduced structure when local rings O_{Z,z} are formed.
Condition (c) is the ring-theoretic predicate Ideal.IsNowhereDense of the suggested file.
The equivalence with (d) is Conrad's formulation for Tate's rigid spaces; on a quasi-separated X it is transported through Huber's functor.
proofSteps: (a) ⇔ (b): affinoid opens (rational subsets) form a basis of |X| and are nonempty when their coordinate ring is nonzero.

(b) ⇒ (c): if I ⊆ p for a minimal prime p of A, choose g lying in every other minimal prime but not in p (prime avoidance). g is not nilpotent, so its supremum norm is positive (AdicSpacesPartII:R0/affinoid-maximum-modulus) and for c ∈ K× with |c| ≤ |g|_sup the Laurent domain {|g| ≥ |c|} is a nonempty affinoid open. At each of its points x, supp(x) does not contain g, so it contains the minimal prime p; hence the domain lies in V(p) ⊆ V(I) = Z.

(c) ⇒ (b): if Z ⊇ U = Spa(B, B°) ≠ ∅ inside Spa(A, A°), then I·B is nilpotent; B has a minimal prime q and A → B is flat (AdicSpacesPartII:R1/affinoid-subdomain-flat), so by going down q ∩ A is a minimal prime of A containing I.

(c) ⇔ (d): at a classical point z with maximal ideal m, the completions of A_m and O_{X,z} agree (AdicSpacesPartII:R1/rigid-local-ring-completion), so dimensions may be computed in A_m; dim (A/I)_m < dim A_m for all m ⊇ I iff no minimal prime of A contained in m contains I, by catenarity of the excellent ring A (SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.0/excellent-ring) and the equidimensionality of affinoid domains (AdicSpacesPartII:R1/affinoid-domain-equidimensional).

For the dimension criterion, work with the finite minimal primes p_i of an affinoid A. A closed subset containing V(p_i) has the same local dimension at a classical point of that component away from the other components. Conversely, if I is contained in none of the p_i, each closed subset V(I+p_i) has dimension strictly smaller than the equidimensional affinoid domain A/p_i; localizing and taking the maximum over the components through a point gives strict local dimension drop. This is the affinoid argument in Conrad §2.1, p. 10.

nodes.title: Images of proper morphisms are Zariski closed
nodes.statement: Let f : Y → X be a proper morphism of rigid spaces over K. Then f(|Y|) is a Zariski closed subset of X, namely the support of the coherent O_X-module f_*O_Y; its reduced structure is the closed subspace defined by ker(O_X → f_*O_Y) up to radical. More generally, for a Zariski closed T ⊆ Y, f(T) is Zariski closed in X.
hypotheses: f proper in the sense of AdicSpacesPartII:R0/universally-closed-and-proper-morphism; no reducedness or smoothness is assumed.
proofSteps: By Kiehl's proper mapping theorem (AdicSpacesPartII:R3/kiehl-proper-mapping-theorem) f_*O_Y is coherent, so its support is Zariski closed (support of a coherent sheaf = V of its annihilator ideal, AdicSpacesPartII:R3/coherent-sheaf).
Supp(f_*O_Y) ⊆ f(|Y|): if x ∉ f(|Y|) then, f being closed, a neighbourhood of x misses f(|Y|) and f_*O_Y vanishes there.
f(|Y|) ⊆ Supp(f_*O_Y): if (f_*O_Y)_x = 0, the section 1 of f_*O_Y vanishes on an open V′ ∋ x, so 1 = 0 in O_Y(f^{-1}V′) and f^{-1}V′ = ∅; hence x ∉ f(|Y|).
For T = V(𝓙) apply the result to the proper composite V(𝓙) ↪ Y → X.
acceptance: The image of a closed immersion is its Zariski closed image; the image of the analytified projection P^1 × D → D is all of D.

nodes.title: Affinoid localizations are regular ring maps
nodes.statement: Let K be complete, nontrivially nonarchimedean of rank one. An inclusion Spa(B, B°) ⊆ Spa(A, A°) of affinoid domains induces a regular ring map A → B: it is flat and has geometrically regular fibres. Smooth morphisms of K-affinoid spaces also induce regular ring maps. The proof uses excellence of K-affinoid algebras in every characteristic; the cited parent node supplies this only in characteristic zero, and request Q1 records the remaining extension.
hypotheses: No perfectness or characteristic assumption on K in the target. Q1 is required outside characteristic zero.
At a classical point of an affinoid subdomain the completed local coordinate rings agree with the completed rigid stalk.
proofSteps: Flatness: AdicSpacesPartII:R1/affinoid-subdomain-flat.
At a maximal ideal m′ of A′ over m ⊆ A, A_m → A′_{m′} induces an isomorphism of completions (AdicSpacesPartII:R1/rigid-local-ring-completion and Conrad, proof of Corollary 1.2.3).

A_m → Â_m is regular (A excellent), and Â_m ≅ Â′_{m′} is faithfully flat over A′_{m′}; by descent of regularity along faithfully flat maps (the composite A_m → A′_{m′} → Â′_{m′} is regular), A_m → A′_{m′} is regular.
Every prime of A′ lies in a maximal ideal (A′ is Jacobson), so the fibres of A → A′ are localizations of those just treated.
Smooth case: étale-locally over a relative polydisc A⟨T_1, …, T_n⟩, and A → A⟨T⟩ is regular by the same completion argument with power series rings.
acceptance: K⟨T⟩ → K⟨T, T^{-1}⟩ (inclusion of the unit circle) is regular; K⟨T⟩ → K (evaluation at 0) is not flat, hence not regular.

sources.match: Records that the maps from the coordinate rings of affinoid charts to those of their intersections' affinoid pieces are regular homomorphisms of excellent rings.
For an open immersion of affinoids, the local maps at maximal ideals induce isomorphisms of completions, hence are faithfully flat.

Affinoid excellence holds in every characteristic; classical stalks are excellent and have the same completions as maximal localizations. These supply the completion and descent argument for regular domain inclusions.

nodes.title: The normalization of a rigid space
nodes.statement: Let X be a rigid space over K. For an affinoid open U = Spa(A, A°), let Ã^ν be the integral closure of A_red in its total ring of fractions; it is a finite A-algebra and a K-affinoid algebra. For affinoid opens V ⊆ U the natural map O(V) ⊗_{O(U)} O(U)^ν → O(V)^ν is an isomorphism (Conrad, Corollary 1.2.3), so the finite morphisms Spa(O(U)^ν) → U glue to a finite surjective morphism p : X^ν → X, the normalization of X. X^ν is normal (every local ring is a normal domain), p factors through X_red, the factor X^ν → X_red is an isomorphism over the normal locus of X_red, and a morphism Y → X is called a normalization if it is isomorphic over X to p (the isomorphism is then unique).
hypotheses: Finiteness uses excellence (hence the Nagata property) of affinoid algebras. AdicSpacesPartII:F1/dagger-algebra-excellent supplies characteristic zero; Q1 requests the all-characteristic statement recalled by Conrad §1.1, p. 3.
Conrad works on Tate's rigid spaces; the construction is local, so it applies verbatim on the adic side and is compatible with Huber's functor.
proofSteps: Affinoid case: Ã^ν is a finite A-module (A excellent, hence Nagata and Japanese, SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.0/excellent-ring) and a quotient of a Tate algebra, hence affinoid; Spa(Ã^ν) → Spa(A) is finite (AdicSpacesPartII:R0/finite-algebra-over-affinoid).

Compatibility with affinoid subdomains (Conrad Theorem 1.2.2 and Corollary 1.2.3): A → A′ = O(V) is flat with A_n → A′_m inducing isomorphisms of completions at classical points, A′ ⊗_A Ã^ν is normal because Spa of it is an open of the normal space Spa(Ã^ν), and A′/p is reduced for minimal primes p of A; Conrad's Theorem 1.2.2 then says A′ → A′ ⊗_A Ã^ν is the normalization of A′.

Glue the affinoid normalizations along these canonical isomorphisms (AdicSpacesPartII:R3/finite-morphism-coherent-algebra-equivalence: finite morphisms are coherent O_X-algebras, so gluing is gluing of a coherent algebra).
Stalks (Conrad Lemma 2.1.1): (p_*O_{X^ν})_x is the normalization of O_{X,x}_red and is the product of the normal domains O_{X^ν,y} over y ∈ p^{-1}(x).

The normalization of Spa(K⟨X,Y⟩/(XY)) is the disjoint union of two discs; that of a normal space is the identity.

nodes.title: Conrad's characterization of normalizations
nodes.statement: A morphism f : Y → X of reduced rigid spaces over K is a normalization if and only if f is finite, Y is normal, and there is a nowhere dense Zariski closed Z ⊆ X with f^{-1}(Z) nowhere dense in Y such that f is an isomorphism over X − Z. When f is a normalization, O_X → f_*O_Y is injective and Z may be taken to be the support of its coherent cokernel, which is the non-normal locus of X.
hypotheses: X and Y reduced; nowhere density in the sense of AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.0/nowhere-dense-criteria.
proofSteps: If f is a normalization: O_X → f_*O_Y is a monomorphism of coherent sheaves because X is reduced; the support Z of the cokernel is the non-normal locus, which is Zariski closed and nowhere dense with nowhere dense preimage by the corresponding facts for the excellent reduced coordinate rings (Conrad, proof of Theorem 2.1.2).

Conversely, work over an affinoid X = Spa(A); then Y = Spa(B) with A → B finite. It is injective: a function vanishing off the nowhere dense Z has zero locus containing a nonempty open, hence everywhere (RZ.0), and A is reduced.
Away from V(I) (I the radical ideal of Z), A_m → B_m is an isomorphism at maximal ideals: it is finite, and an isomorphism after the faithfully flat completion because f is an isomorphism over X − Z.
Since no minimal prime of A contains I and none of B contains IB, A → B is an isomorphism at generic points; a finite injection into a normal ring that is birational is the normalization.
acceptance: The map t ↦ (t², t³) from the disc to the cuspidal disc satisfies the criterion with Z the cusp.

nodes.title: Connected components of a rigid space
nodes.statement: A rigid space X over K is connected if it is nonempty and admits no covering by two disjoint nonempty open subspaces; equivalently it is nonempty and O_X(X) has no idempotents other than 0 and 1. The connected component of x ∈ |X| is the union of all connected open subspaces containing x; it is an open and Zariski closed subspace (clopen), the connected components partition X, a quasi-compact open meets only finitely many of them, and every union of connected components is clopen. They are the connected components of the topological space |X|; on a quasi-separated X they correspond under Huber's functor to Conrad's connected components defined by chains of connected affinoids.
hypotheses: X locally noetherian, so every affinoid open is a finite disjoint union of connected affinoid opens (idempotents of a noetherian ring).
proofSteps: An affinoid Spa(A, A°) is connected iff A ≠ 0 and A has no nontrivial idempotent (sheafiness, AdicSpacesPartII:R0/noetherian-type-stably-sheafy), and A = ∏ A e_i splits it into finitely many connected affinoids; so connected affinoid opens form a basis and |X| is locally connected.
Hence topological connected components of |X| are open; being closed, each is the support of the idempotent ideal it defines, hence Zariski closed.
Local finiteness: a quasi-compact open is a finite union of affinoids, each meeting finitely many components.
Comparison with Conrad (§2.1, p. 11): chains of connected affinoids linking two points give the same equivalence relation as topological connectedness, by local connectedness.

nodes.title: Irreducible components of a rigid space
nodes.statement: Let p : X^ν → X be the normalization of a rigid space X over K. The irreducible components of X are the Zariski closed subsets X_i = p(X^ν_i), with their reduced structure, for X^ν_i running through the connected components of X^ν. X is irreducible if it is nonempty and has exactly one irreducible component; a Zariski closed subset Z is irreducible if Z_red is. The components cover X, are locally finite, and X_i ≠ X_j for i ≠ j.
hypotheses: Defined through the normalization, not through the Zariski topology: the Zariski topology of a rigid space is not noetherian, and irreducibility in its sense is the criterion RZ.1/irreducibility-criterion.

Local analytic branches are not the global components through a point. A globally irreducible space can have a reducible analytic stalk. The component comparison under analytification is imported as a separate comparison from the parent, not used to construct components.
proofSteps: Images: p is finite, so p(X^ν_i) is Zariski closed (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.0/proper-image-zariski-closed).

Distinctness and generic normality (Conrad Lemma 2.2.1): p^{-1}(p(U)) − U is nowhere dense for a clopen U ⊆ X^ν; each X_i contains a nonempty Zariski open subset, normal and disjoint from the other components, over which p is an isomorphism; p_i : X^ν_i → X_i is a normalization (RZ.1/normalization-characterisation).

Hence components of X correspond bijectively to connected components of X^ν (Conrad Theorem 2.2.4(1)), every irreducible Zariski closed subset lies in a component (2.2.4(2)), and a union of components is the image of the corresponding union of components of X^ν, which is its normalization (2.2.4(3)).
Local finiteness: a quasi-compact open of X has quasi-compact preimage in X^ν (p finite), which meets finitely many connected components.

Over a complete field of characteristic zero, the analytification of the integral cubic y² = x²(x+1) is globally irreducible. At (0,0), the convergent square root of 1+x factors the equation into two analytic branches, so its analytic local ring has two minimal primes. The normalization has two points over that node (t = ±1 under x=t²−1, y=t(t²−1)).

nodes.title: Irreducible spaces: proper Zariski closed subsets are nowhere dense
nodes.statement: Let X be a nonempty rigid space over K. The following are equivalent: (a) X is irreducible; (b) X is not the union of two proper Zariski closed subsets; (c) the only Zariski closed subset of X containing a nonempty open subset of |X| is X itself. Consequently, if X is irreducible then every Zariski closed Z ⊊ X is nowhere dense: dim O_{Z,z} < dim O_{X,z} at every classical z ∈ Z and dim_z Z < dim_z X at every z ∈ Z. For X connected and normal (in particular smooth and connected) this is the identity principle of AdicSpacesPartII:R1/rigid-identity-principle (Conrad Lemma 2.1.4).
hypotheses: X nonempty. No reducedness is needed: all three conditions depend only on X_red.
proofSteps: (a) ⇒ (b), (c): X^ν is connected and normal and p is surjective; if X = Z_1 ∪ Z_2 then X^ν = p^{-1}Z_1 ∪ p^{-1}Z_2, so one of them is X^ν by the identity principle on X^ν (AdicSpacesPartII:R1/rigid-identity-principle); if Z ⊇ U ≠ ∅ open, p^{-1}Z ⊇ p^{-1}U ≠ ∅, so p^{-1}Z = X^ν.
(b) ⇒ (a): a decomposition of X^ν into two disjoint nonempty clopens U_1, U_2 gives X = p(U_1) ∪ p(U_2); if p(U_1) = X then p^{-1}p(U_1) − U_1 = U_2 is nowhere dense by Conrad Lemma 2.2.1(1), absurd.
(c) ⇒ (b): if X = Z_1 ∪ Z_2 with Z_1 ≠ X, the nonempty Zariski open X − Z_1 lies in Z_2, so Z_2 = X.
Nowhere density of proper Zariski closed subsets is (c) combined with AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.0/nowhere-dense-criteria.
acceptance: In the disc, every proper Zariski closed subset is a discrete set of classical points.
Spa(K⟨X,Y⟩/(XY)) is the union of its two axes, so it is not irreducible, and the axis V(Y) is a proper Zariski closed subset that is not nowhere dense.

nodes.title: Zariski closed subsets of full dimension
nodes.statement: Let X be an irreducible rigid space over K of dimension d. (i) An irreducible Zariski closed Z ⊆ X with dim Z = d equals X; (ii) a Zariski closed Z ⊆ X with dim_z Z = d at some point z equals X. In particular, if X is smooth and connected and Z ⊆ X is Zariski closed with dim_z Z = dim X at one point, then Z = X; and if M is smooth and Y ⊆ M is a connected Zariski closed subset with dim_y Y = dim_y M at some y, then Y is the connected component of M through y.
hypotheses: dim_z Z is the local dimension of Z_red at z (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.0/local-dimension).
proofSteps: An irreducible X has constant finite local dimension d. A proper Zariski closed Z is nowhere dense by the irreducibility criterion; the local dimension criterion then gives dim_z Z < d at every z ∈ Z. Thus dim_z Z = d at even one point forces Z = X.
If dim Z = d, its bounded integer-valued local dimensions attain their supremum d. Apply the preceding argument; this includes the formulation where Z is irreducible.

Smooth case: a smooth connected space is normal and connected, hence irreducible (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.1/irreducible-components), of constant local dimension. For Y ⊆ M connected, apply (ii) in the connected component M_0 ∋ y: Y ⊇ M_0, and Y ⊆ M_0 since Y is connected.
acceptance: In the bidisc, the Zariski closed V(XY) has dimension 1 < 2, so it is a proper subset; a closed subdisc of the disc has full dimension but is not Zariski closed.

nodes.title: Riemann extension theorem for normal rigid spaces
nodes.statement: For a normal rigid space X over K and a nowhere dense analytic subset Z, every bounded analytic function on X − Z extends uniquely to X. K is any complete nontrivially nonarchimedean field; geometric normality is not required.
hypotheses: Bounded means that some real C bounds the absolute value at all rank-one points of X − Z. For disconnected or non-quasi-compact spaces, the local bounded version glues by uniqueness.
proofSteps: Use Bartenwerfer’s general extension theorem, stated in Conrad Theorem 2.1.1. On an affinoid normal neighbourhood the bounded function extends across Z; uniqueness follows from the identity principle, and these local extensions glue.
The extension theorem itself is a substantial input, not a consequence of the identity principle. G1 records that its original proof has not been read.
acceptance: For a connected normal X, an idempotent on X − Z is bounded by 1; its extension is still idempotent by density and the identity principle.
No claim that X becomes connected or normal after extending K is used.

sources.match: States Bartenwerfer’s extension theorem over the original ground field, distinguishing it from Lütkebohmert’s earlier geometric-normality version.

nodes.title: Dense Zariski opens of irreducible spaces are connected
nodes.statement: Let X be a rigid space over K and Z ⊆ X a nowhere dense Zariski closed subset. If X is connected and normal, then X − Z is connected. If X is irreducible, then X − Z is irreducible; in particular every nonempty Zariski open subset of an irreducible rigid space is irreducible and connected.
hypotheses: No geometric connectedness, geometric normality or characteristic-zero hypothesis. Use the original-field Riemann extension theorem.
proofSteps: If X is connected and normal, a disconnection of X − Z supplies a bounded nontrivial idempotent. The Riemann extension theorem extends it to X. Its square minus itself vanishes on the dense complement, hence on X; connectedness forces the extension to be 0 or 1, a contradiction.

For irreducible X, its normalization is connected and normal; the inverse image of Z is nowhere dense. Apply the normal case and use compatibility of normalization with open restriction: the normalization of X − Z is connected, so X − Z is irreducible. Its continuous surjective normalization also proves connectedness.
acceptance: The punctured disc {0 < |T| ≤ 1} is connected.
Removing the node from the analytified nodal cubic leaves a connected space; removing the origin from Spa(K⟨X,Y⟩/(XY)) disconnects it, which is allowed because that space is not irreducible.

nodes.title: The singular locus of a rigid space
nodes.statement: For a rigid space X over K, the singular (non-regular) locus Sing(X) ⊆ |X| is the Zariski closed subset whose trace on each affinoid open Spa(A, A°) is V(J_A), where V(J_A) ⊆ Spec A is the non-regular locus of the excellent ring A (Zariski closed, J_A radical). Its classical points are the classical x with O_{X,x} not regular. Reg(X) = |X| − Sing(X) is the regular locus. If X is reduced, Sing(X) is nowhere dense.
hypotheses: Affinoid excellence in characteristic zero is supplied by AdicSpacesPartII:F1/dagger-algebra-excellent; request Q1 supplies the all-characteristic extension. Excellence makes the non-regular locus closed (J-2) and detects regularity on completions.
proofSteps: For an affinoid A and a classical point x ↔ m, A_m and O_{X,x} have the same completion (AdicSpacesPartII:R1/rigid-local-ring-completion), so O_{X,x} is regular iff A_m is regular iff m ∉ V(J_A).

The earlier regular affinoid-restriction theorem implies that A_m is regular iff the local ring at the corresponding classical point of the affinoid subdomain is regular: regularity ascends along regular maps and descends along faithfully flat local maps. Thus J_A A′ and J_{A′} have the same vanishing locus on classical points; the Jacobson property identifies their radicals, so these closed subsets glue.

Nowhere density for reduced X: a reduced excellent ring is regular at its minimal primes (localizations are fields), so J_A is contained in no minimal prime; apply AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.0/nowhere-dense-criteria(c).
acceptance: Sing of the cuspidal disc is its cusp; Sing of a polydisc is empty.
Sing(Spa(K⟨T⟩/(T²))) is all of |X|: without reducedness the singular locus need not be nowhere dense.

nodes.title: Smooth equals regular in characteristic zero
nodes.statement: Let K have characteristic 0 and X be a rigid space over K. For x ∈ |X|, X → Spa(K, K°) is smooth on a neighbourhood of x if and only if x ∉ Sing(X). At such points Ω_{X/K} is locally free of rank dim_x X, and for a classical point x with residue field k(x) the completed local ring Ô_{X,x} is a formal power series ring over k(x) in dim_x X variables. Hence the smooth locus X^sm is the Zariski open Reg(X), dense when X is reduced.
hypotheses: Characteristic 0 is used only through the separability of every finite extension k(x)/K; over any perfect complete field the same holds (Conrad §3.3).
proofSteps: Smooth morphisms are locally étale over relative polydiscs. At a classical point an étale map gives the corresponding completed local algebra after the finite separable residue-field extension, not necessarily an isomorphism with the unextended target completion. These completions are regular, so the source local ring is regular.

Regular ⇒ smooth at classical points: if O_{X,x} is regular of dimension d with k(x)/K separable, Ô_{X,x} ≅ k(x)⟦t_1, …, t_d⟧, so Ω_{X/K,x} ⊗ Ô_{X,x} is free of rank d; hence Ω_{X/K} is free of rank d near x, and the Jacobian criterion (AdicSpacesPartII:R0/jacobian-criterion-closed-subspace, in a local closed embedding into a polydisc) gives smoothness near x (Conrad, proof of Lemma 3.3.1, citing Bosch–Lütkebohmert III, Lemma 2.8(b)).
Both loci are open and Zariski open; a Zariski open set is determined by its classical points (Jacobson), so they coincide.
Rank: on a smooth neighbourhood, rank Ω = dim of the étale-local polydisc = dim_x X (AdicSpacesPartII:R0/smooth-differentials-locally-free).
acceptance: The smooth locus of the analytified nodal cubic is the complement of the node.
Over an imperfect field of characteristic p the statement fails: Spa(k⟨T⟩[Y]/(Y^p − a)) with a ∉ k^p is regular but not smooth.

nodes.title: Tangent spaces and differentials at classical points
nodes.statement: Let X be a rigid space over K and x a classical point with residue field k(x). The Zariski tangent space is T_x X = Hom_{k(x)}(m_x/m_x², k(x)), m_x ⊆ O_{X,x}. A morphism f : X → Y induces df_x : T_x X → T_{f(x)} Y ⊗_{k(f(x))} k(x). If k(x) = K (or k(x)/K is separable), T_x X is dual to Ω_{X/K} ⊗ k(x); for a K-rational point of a smooth X, dim T_x X = dim_x X, and df_x is the fibre at x of the dual of f^*Ω_{Y/K} → Ω_{X/K}. For L/K a complete extension and x ∈ X(L), T_x X_L is defined the same way on X_L = X ×_K Spa L.
hypotheses: Tangent spaces are taken at classical points (or L-points after base change); no tangent space is defined at non-classical points.
proofSteps: m_x/m_x² is finite over k(x) because O_{X,x} is noetherian; the completion does not change it (AdicSpacesPartII:R1/rigid-local-ring-completion).
Functoriality and the chain rule: f^♯ : O_{Y,f(x)} → O_{X,x} is local, inducing m_{f(x)}/m_{f(x)}² ⊗ k(x) → m_x/m_x², whose dual is df_x; composition is respected.

Comparison with differentials at a rational point: the map m_x/m_x² → Ω_{X/K} ⊗ k(x), g ↦ dg, is an isomorphism for k(x) = K (continuous differentials, AdicSpacesPartII:R3/sheaf-of-continuous-differentials).
Smooth case: Ω_{X/K} is locally free of rank dim_x X (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.2/smooth-iff-regular).
acceptance: For f : D → D, z ↦ z² over K of characteristic ≠ 2, df_a is multiplication by 2a: zero exactly at the origin.
At the cusp of Spa(K⟨X,Y⟩/(Y² − X³)) the tangent space has dimension 2 while the space has dimension 1.

nodes.title: Stratification of a reduced space by smooth locally closed subspaces
nodes.statement: Let K have characteristic 0 and Y be a reduced rigid space over K of finite dimension d (not necessarily quasi-compact). Put Y_0 = Y and Y_{i+1} = Sing(Y_i) with its reduced structure. Then dim Y_{i+1} < dim Y_i whenever Y_i ≠ ∅, so Y_{d+1} = ∅, and |Y| is the disjoint union of the finitely many locally closed subspaces Y_i − Y_{i+1} (0 ≤ i ≤ d), each smooth over K and Zariski open in the Zariski closed Y_i. Every point of Y lies on exactly one stratum.
hypotheses: Finite dimension, not quasi-compactness, makes the stratification finite (the review of the Howe–Klevdal extraction corrected the hypothesis).
Characteristic 0 identifies Y_i − Y_{i+1} = Reg(Y_i) with the smooth locus.
proofSteps: Y_i is reduced and Zariski closed in Y; Sing(Y_i) is nowhere dense in Y_i (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.2/singular-locus), so dim_z Y_{i+1} < dim_z Y_i at every z ∈ Y_{i+1} (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.0/nowhere-dense-criteria(e)), whence dim Y_{i+1} ≤ dim Y_i − 1.
Y_i − Y_{i+1} = Reg(Y_i) is smooth over K (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.2/smooth-iff-regular) and open in Y_i.
Disjointness and covering: z ∈ Y lies in Y_i − Y_{i+1} for the largest i with z ∈ Y_i.
acceptance: For the union of a plane and a line meeting it in a point inside the 3-dimensional polydisc, Y_1 is the intersection point and Y_2 = ∅.
For the cuspidal disc, the strata are the punctured cuspidal curve and the cusp.

nodes.title: Zariski-open loci of maximal rank of a differential
nodes.statement: Let f : V → W be a morphism of smooth rigid spaces over K. For r ≥ 0 let V_{≥r} be the set of x ∈ |V| at which the map f^*Ω_{W/K} ⊗ k(x) → Ω_{V/K} ⊗ k(x) has rank ≥ r. Then V_{≥r} is Zariski open: locally, in coordinates where Ω_V and Ω_W are free, it is the complement of the common zero locus of the r × r minors of the Jacobian matrix. If V is connected and r_max = max_x rank, then V_{≥r_max} is a nonempty Zariski open subset whose complement is nowhere dense, and on it rank df_x = r_max at every classical point x (rank of df_x on T_x V_{k(x)}).
hypotheses: V, W smooth over K, so Ω_V and Ω_W are locally free of finite rank (AdicSpacesPartII:R0/smooth-differentials-locally-free).

Define rank at every point using the fibre of f^*Ω_{W/K} → Ω_{V/K}. Its dual agrees with the map on m/m² tangent spaces at rational points and at classical points with separable residue extension; do not assert this comparison at arbitrary inseparable classical points.
proofSteps: Locally Ω_V and f^*Ω_W are free with bases dT_j, f^*dS_i; the map is given by the Jacobian matrix (∂f_i/∂T_j), and rank ≥ r at x iff some r × r minor does not vanish at x; the ideal of minors is coherent, so V_{≥r} is Zariski open.
Rank is lower semicontinuous and bounded by dim W, so r_max is attained; V_{≥r_max} is nonempty Zariski open.

Its complement is a proper Zariski closed subset of the connected smooth, hence irreducible, V (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.1/irreducible-components), so it is nowhere dense (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.1/irreducibility-criterion).
On V_{≥r_max} the rank is ≥ r_max and ≤ r_max, hence constant.
The algebraic core over a field is the minor criterion for the rank of a matrix (suggested name Matrix.le_rank_iff_exists_submatrix_det_ne_zero).
acceptance: For f(z) = z² on the disc (char K ≠ 2), V_{≥1} = D − {0} and r_max = 1.
For a constant map V_{≥0} = V and r_max = 0; for the identity of D^n, r_max = n everywhere.

nodes.title: Classical points and L-points of a rigid space
nodes.statement: Let X be a rigid space over K. A point x ∈ |X| is classical if its residue field k(x) = O_{X,x}/m_x is a finite extension of K (equivalently its completed residue field is finite over K). For a finite extension L/K, X(L) = Hom_{Spa K}(Spa(L, L°), X); a morphism Spa L → X has classical image x together with a K-embedding k(x) ↪ L, and this gives a bijection between X(L) and such pairs. On an affinoid open Spa(A, A°) the classical points are the image of the injective map Max A → Spa(A, A°), m ↦ the absolute value |·| of A/m extended uniquely from K. The classical points of X are the points of the classical rigid space attached to X by Huber's functor when X is quasi-separated.
hypotheses: Only finite extensions L/K are used for L-points here; for a complete algebraically closed C ⊇ K, X(C) is defined in AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.6 through X_C.

k(x) denotes the residue field of the analytic local ring; H(x) denotes its completion. At classical points they coincide since finite extensions of K are complete. For a Gauss point η, H(η) is the Gauss-norm completion of the rational function field; do not identify that completion with an uncompleted residue field.
proofSteps: Max A → Spa(A, A°): for a maximal ideal m, A/m is a finite field extension of K (AdicSpacesPartII:R0/affinoid-residue-fields-finite) with a unique absolute value extending that of K; the induced valuation is continuous and ≤ 1 on A°.
Injectivity: its support is m.

Conversely a point x with k(x) finite over K has support a prime p with A/p ↪ k(x) finite over K, so A/p is a field and p is maximal; the valuation on k(x) is the unique extension, so x is the image of p.
L-points: a morphism Spa(L, L°) → Spa(A, A°) over K is a continuous K-algebra map A → L, whose kernel is a maximal ideal; this gives the bijection with pairs (x, k(x) ↪ L).
acceptance: On the closed unit disc over Q_p, T = √p is a classical point with residue field Q_p(√p) and |T| = p^{−1/2}; the Gauss point is not classical.
If x ∈ X is classical then so is f(x) for every morphism f of rigid spaces.

nodes.title: Rigid analytic points of a diamond
nodes.statement: Let L be a complete nonarchimedean field over Q_p and S a diamond over Spd L = Spa(L, L°)^♢. A rigid analytic point of S over L is a pair (L′, s) of a finite extension L′/L and a morphism s : Spd L′ → S over Spd L. Two rigid analytic points (L′, s), (L″, s′) are equivalent if there are a finite extension L‴/L and L-embeddings L′, L″ ↪ L‴ with s ∘ Spd(L‴ → L′) = s′ ∘ Spd(L‴ → L″); this generates an equivalence relation. The image of (L′, s) is the point |s|(|Spd L′|) ∈ |S|, which depends only on the equivalence class.
hypotheses: Spd L′ = Spa(L′, L′°)^♢ has a single point, so the image is a single point of |S|.
Howe–Klevdal also define rigid analytic diamonds and subdiamonds (Definition 2.2.1(2)–(3)); those belong to the roadmap on admissible pairs, which imports this definition.
proofSteps: The diamond Spd L′ and the maps Spd(L‴) → Spd(L′) for L-embeddings come from the functor Y ↦ Y^♢ on analytic adic spaces (DiamondsAndVStacks:D6/gluing-and-the-diamond-functor).
|Spd L′| = |Spa L′| is a point (DiamondsAndVStacks:D6/etale-site-comparison), so the image is well defined, and equivalent pairs have the same image by functoriality of |·|.

Equivalence is reflexive and symmetric; take the generated equivalence relation (it is already transitive by composing embeddings into a common finite extension, which exists inside an algebraic closure of L).
acceptance: Spd L has the identity as a rigid analytic point; a map Spd C → S from a completed algebraic closure C is not one.

nodes.title: Classical points are the rigid analytic points of the diamond
nodes.statement: Let L be a complete nonarchimedean field over Q_p and Y a rigid space over L. Under |Y^♢| = |Y|, the image of every rigid analytic point of Y^♢ over Spd L is a classical point of Y, and s ↦ image induces a bijection between equivalence classes of rigid analytic points of Y^♢ and classical points of Y. For each finite L′/L, the rigid analytic points with source Spd L′ are in bijection with Y(L′).
hypotheses: Y need not be seminormal: the map Spa(L′) → Y attached to s exists because Spa L′ is normal, hence seminormal, and maps out of seminormal rigid spaces are detected on diamonds (DiamondsAndVStacks:D6/seminormal-rigid-full-faithfulness, whose source is seminormal and target arbitrary).
proofSteps: By seminormal full faithfulness, Hom_{Spd L}(Spd L′, Y^♢) = Hom_{Spa L}(Spa L′, Y) = Y(L′) (DiamondsAndVStacks:D6/seminormal-rigid-full-faithfulness).
By AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.3/classical-point, Y(L′) is the set of pairs (x classical, k(x) ↪ L′); the image point in |Y| = |Y^♢| (DiamondsAndVStacks:D6/etale-site-comparison) is x.

Two rigid analytic points have the same image iff they are equivalent: if both lie over x, embed L′ and L″ over k(x) into a common finite L‴; then both restrictions are the map attached to (x, k(x) ↪ L‴), up to choosing the embeddings compatibly; conversely equivalent points have the same image.
Surjectivity: a classical x gives (k(x), the canonical map Spd k(x) → Y^♢).
acceptance: For the closed unit disc over L, the rigid analytic points over L′ are the elements of O_{L′}, and their classes are the Gal(L̄/L)-orbits of elements of O_{L̄} algebraic over L, i.e. the classical points.
For the B_dR^+-affine Grassmannian (not a rigid analytic diamond) the analogous statement fails: its only rigid analytic point is 0.

nodes.title: The L-points of a polydisc with the subspace topology
nodes.statement: Let L be a complete nonarchimedean field with nontrivial absolute value and D = Spa(L⟨T_1, …, T_n⟩, L°⟨T_1, …, T_n⟩) the closed unit polydisc. The map O_L^n → |D|, a ↦ the classical point T = a, is injective, and with the subspace topology on its image D(L) ⊆ |D| it is a homeomorphism onto D(L) from O_L^n with its valuation topology. Hence D(L) is a complete metric space and a Baire space.
hypotheses: L is not required to be discretely valued; the polydisc is the unit one.
proofSteps: Injectivity: distinct a, b ∈ O_L^n give distinct maximal ideals (T − a) and (T − b).

A rational domain pulls back to inequalities |f_i(a)| ≤ |g(a)| ≠ 0. Around an a satisfying them, choose a small ball on which |g| is constant and each f_i changes by less than |g(a)|. The ultrametric inequality preserves the weak inequalities on that ball. Thus the inverse image is open; ordinary continuity alone would not justify weak inequalities.
Openness onto the image: the ball {|T_i − a_i| ≤ |c|} (c ∈ L^×) is a rational subset whose L-points are exactly the corresponding ball of O_L^n; balls form a basis of O_L^n.

O_L^n is closed in the complete finite product L^n, so it is complete. Obtain its BaireSpace instance by Mathlib typeclass inference (the source-checked instance BaireSpace.of_completelyPseudoMetrizable, Mathlib/Topology/Baire/CompleteMetrizable.lean, line 26). No separate analytic Baire theorem is planned.
acceptance: D(L) ⊆ |D| is not closed when n ≥ 1: its closure contains the Gauss point if the residue field is infinite (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.3/gauss-point-in-closure).
For n = 0, D(L) is the single point Spa L.

nodes.title: A closed set containing the rational points of a disc contains its Gauss point
nodes.statement: Let L be a complete nonarchimedean field whose residue field L̃ is infinite, D the closed unit polydisc of dimension n over L and η ∈ |D| its Gauss point, the rank-one point |Σ a_α T^α|_η = max_α |a_α|. Then every open neighbourhood of η in |D| contains L-points; more precisely a rational neighbourhood {|f_i| ≤ |g|} of η normalised so that |g|_η = 1 (so g ∈ L°⟨T⟩ with nonzero reduction ḡ ∈ L̃[T]) contains every a ∈ O_L^n whose reduction ā satisfies ḡ(ā) ≠ 0, and such a exist. Consequently a closed subset of |D| containing D(L) contains η, and a closed subset of a rigid space S containing a polydisc's worth of L-points (the L-points of an open polydisc neighbourhood of an L-point) contains the corresponding Gauss point. If L̃ is finite the conclusion fails.
hypotheses: L̃ infinite is exactly what is used. Howe–Klevdal apply it with L′ finite over a p-adic field containing Q̆_p, whose residue field contains F̄_p (they write that the residue field is algebraically closed; only infinitude is needed — source issue recorded by the paper extraction).

Reuse the current Tau Ceti one-variable Gauss-point construction; its existence is not new work. The multivariable closure theorem remains a target. Current-library evidence is separate from the pinned baseline.
proofSteps: Normalise: at η, |g|_η = 1 > 0, so scaling makes g ∈ L°⟨T⟩ with Gauss norm 1; then |f_i|_η ≤ 1 forces f_i ∈ L°⟨T⟩.

Its reduction ḡ ∈ L̃[T_1, …, T_n] is a nonzero polynomial; since L̃ is infinite, ḡ(ā) ≠ 0 for some ā ∈ L̃^n (Mathlib MvPolynomial.funext over an infinite field); lift to a ∈ O_L^n (over any local ring with infinite residue field: suggested name MvPolynomial.exists_isUnit_eval_of_infinite_residueField).
Then |g(a)| = 1 and |f_i(a)| ≤ 1 = |g(a)|, so x_a lies in the neighbourhood.
Rational subsets containing η form a neighbourhood basis of η, so every open neighbourhood of η meets D(L); a closed set containing D(L) contains η.
Failure for finite L̃ = F_q, n = 1: the rational subset {|T^q − T| ≥ 1} = {1 ≤ |T^q − T|} contains η (|T^q − T|_η = 1) but no point of O_L, where |a^q − a| < 1.
acceptance: Over L = Q_p^{ur}-completion (residue field F̄_p), the open neighbourhood {|T| ≥ 1} ∩ {|T − 1| ≥ 1} of η contains the L-point T = ζ for a root of unity ζ ≠ 1 of order prime to p.
Over Q_p (residue field F_p), {|T^p − T| ≥ 1} is an open neighbourhood of the Gauss point of the disc containing no Q_p-point.

nodes.title: Reduction of an affinoid and the specialisation map
nodes.statement: For a K-affinoid algebra A, let A° be its power-bounded elements, A°° the topologically nilpotent ones and Ã = A°/A°°, a K̃-algebra of finite type. The specialisation map sp : Spa(A, A°) → Spec Ã sends x to the prime ideal {a ∈ A° : |a(x)| < 1}/A°°. It is continuous and surjective, functorial for morphisms of affinoids (through φ̃ : Ã → B̃), sends classical points to closed points, and for the closed unit polydisc sends the Gauss point to the generic point of Spec K̃[T_1, …, T_n].
hypotheses: Ã is of finite type over K̃ by BGR 6.3.4 (finite affinoid maps induce finite reductions, AdicSpacesPartII:R0/affinoid-reduction-finite, applied to a Noether normalization).
proofSteps: sp(x) is prime: {a ∈ A° : |a(x)| < 1} is the preimage of the maximal ideal of the valuation ring of x, and contains A°° because topologically nilpotent elements have |a(x)| < 1.
Continuity: for a ∈ A°, sp^{-1}(D(ā)) = {x : |a(x)| ≥ 1} = {x : |a(x)| = 1}, a rational subset, hence open.

Surjectivity: every prime of Ã is the centre of a valuation of Frac(Ã/q) ⊇ … ; lifting through a formal model whose special fibre maps homeomorphically to Spec Ã (Bhatt–Hansen, first observation in the proof of Proposition 2.2; Raynaud, AdicSpacesPartII:R2/raynaud-theorem) and using that the specialisation of the formal model is surjective.
Functoriality: φ(A°) ⊆ B°, φ(A°°) ⊆ B°° (AdicSpacesPartII:R0/affinoid-reduction-finite) and sp_A ∘ Spa(φ) = Spec(φ̃) ∘ sp_B.
A classical point maps to a maximal ideal: its residue field is finite over K, so the image is a point whose residue field is finite over K̃.
acceptance: For A = K⟨T⟩, Ã = K̃[T], sp(η) is the generic point and sp(x_a) is the closed point T − ā.
For A = K⟨X, Y⟩/(XY − c), 0 < |c| < 1, Ã = K̃[X, Y]/(XY) has two generic points.

nodes.title: Four characterizations of Shilov points
nodes.statement: Let A be a K-affinoid algebra and x ∈ Spa(A, A°) a rank-one point. The following are equivalent: (1) sp(x) is the generic point of an irreducible component of Spec Ã; (2) {x} = sp^{-1}(sp(x)); (3) the valuation ring K_x^+ of the completed residue field of x is the t-adic completion of the local ring of Spec A° at sp(x) (t a pseudo-uniformizer of K); (4) the seminorm |·|_x lies in the Shilov boundary of the Banach K-algebra A.
hypotheses: A is K-affinoid; the equivalences fail for general complete Tate rings (Bhatt–Hansen, Remark 2.3: a perfectoid counterexample).
proofSteps: Choose an open bounded topologically finitely presented K°-subalgebra A_0 ⊆ A° with A° integral over A_0 and Spec Ã → Spec(A_0/t) a universal homeomorphism (Noether normalization and BGR 6.3.4); describe Spa(A, A°) as the limit of the special fibres of proper t-isomorphisms X_i → Spec A_0, with O^+ the t-completed colimit of structure sheaves.

(1) ⇒ (2): localize A° at the inverse image p of the generic point in Ã. It is this localization (or its separated t-adic completion), not the local ring of Ã, that supplies the rank-one valuation ring via affinoid Noether normalization. The latter ring has t=0 and cannot have t as a uniformizer. The valuation-theoretic argument then forces the fibre of sp to be a singleton; see E6.

(2) ⇒ (3): the local rings of the X_i at the unique preimages are integral over A_{0,sp(x)} and isomorphisms after inverting t; the t-completed colimit is integrally closed, hence equals the completed local ring of A°.
(3) ⇒ (2): points of Spa are classes of maps A_0 → V to t-complete valuation rings.

(2) ⇒ (1): if sp(x) were not generic, a valuation of the function field of a component through it, centred at sp(x), composed with K_y^+ for a lift y of the generic point, gives a rank ≥ 2 point over sp(x) different from x.
(1) ⇔ (4): Berkovich, Spectral theory, Proposition 2.4.4.
acceptance: For the disc, (2) holds at η: only η specialises to the generic point; for a classical point the fibre sp^{-1}(sp(x)) is a whole residue disc.

sources.match: For a tft K-algebra and a rank-one point, specialisation to a generic point of Spec Ã, being the only point over its specialisation, K_x^+ being a t-completed localization of A°, and lying in the Shilov boundary are equivalent; the last via Berkovich 2.4.4.

nodes.title: Weakly Shilov points of a rigid space
nodes.statement: Let X be a rigid space over K. A point x ∈ |X| is weakly Shilov if there is an affinoid open W ⊆ X containing x such that x is a Shilov point of W. Weakly Shilov points have rank one. They are dense in |X|: every nonempty affinoid open contains one (Bhatt–Hansen, Lemma 2.8).
hypotheses: X is any rigid space over K; no quasi-separatedness.
proofSteps: Rank one: Shilov points have rank one by definition.

Density: a nonempty open subset contains a nonempty affinoid open W, and Spec W̃ has a generic point; its preimage under the surjective sp is nonempty and consists of a single rank-one point (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.4/shilov-point-characterisation), which is Shilov in W.
acceptance: The weakly Shilov points of the closed unit disc are exactly its type 2 points; type 1, 3, 4 and 5 points are not (Bhatt–Hansen, Example 2.6).

nodes.title: Abhyankar's bound for secondary residue fields
nodes.statement: Let X be a rigid space over K and x ∈ |X| a rank-one point with completed residue field H(x) and secondary residue field K̃_x (the residue field of its valuation ring). Then K̃_x is a field extension of K̃ with trdeg_{K̃} K̃_x ≤ dim_x X.
hypotheses: x of rank one; dim_x X the local dimension (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.0/local-dimension).
proofSteps: Choose an affinoid neighbourhood Spa(A, A°) with dim A = dim_x X =: d and a finite injective K⟨T_1, …, T_e⟩ → A/supp(x) with e = dim A/supp(x) ≤ d (AdicSpacesPartII:R0/affinoid-noether-normalisation).
The image y of x in the e-dimensional polydisc has H(x) finite over H(y), so K̃_x is algebraic over K̃_y.

The dense polynomial algebra shows that the secondary residue field of H(y) is the residue field of the restricted valuation on Frac(K[T]/supp(y)). Lift any finite algebraically independent family of residue classes to units of this valued function field. A polynomial relation among these lifts over K, after dividing its coefficients by one of maximal norm, would reduce to a nonzero relation among their residues over K̃. Thus the lifts are algebraically independent over K, so their number is at most the transcendence degree of this function field, at most e.
acceptance: At the Gauss point of the polydisc, K̃_x = K̃(T_1, …, T_n) has transcendence degree n = dim; at a classical point it is a finite extension of K̃.

sources.match: Characterizes weakly Shilov points by the transcendence degree of the secondary residue field equalling the local dimension, citing Poineau's Lemme 4.4 and Corollaire 4.15, of which the inequality is the first half.
Uses the full Abhyankar inequality. The residue-transcendence inequality needed here is proved directly in the sketch by lifting algebraically independent residues.

nodes.title: Weakly Shilov points are those of maximal residue transcendence degree
nodes.statement: Let X be a rigid space over K and x ∈ |X| a rank-one point. The following are equivalent: (1) x is weakly Shilov; (2) trdeg_{K̃} K̃_x = dim_x X; (3) when X is quasi-separated and quasi-paracompact, there is a formal model 𝔛 of X such that x specialises to the generic point of an irreducible component of the special fibre 𝔛_s.
hypotheses: (3) needs Raynaud's theory of formal models (AdicSpacesPartII:R2/raynaud-theorem), hence quasi-separated and quasi-paracompact X.
proofSteps: For a Shilov point of a strict affinoid neighbourhood, Poineau Lemma 4.4 identifies the residue transcendence degree with the local dimension. Dimension is invariant under open restriction.

Conversely, choose an affinoid neighbourhood U of x whose dimension is d = dim_x X. If trdeg K̃_x = d, Abhyankar’s inequality excludes every lower-dimensional component and every intersection of distinct d-dimensional components through x. Thus x lies on exactly one component of U, of dimension d.

Apply Poineau Corollary 4.18 (and Corollary 4.15 in the irreducible case): there is a strict Laurent domain in U having x as its unique Shilov-boundary point. A strict Laurent domain is a rational affinoid open on the adic side. Proposition 2.2 of Bhatt–Hansen identifies the Berkovich Shilov boundary with the rank-one adic Shilov points. No field extension or descent of a chosen domain is needed.

For the formal-model characterization, use Raynaud’s equivalence and admissible blow-ups to make the chosen affinoid domain a formal open; the generic point of its special fibre gives the desired specialization. This invokes the precise formal-model localization input recorded in G5.
acceptance: At a type 3 point of the disc trdeg = 0 < 1: not weakly Shilov; at type 2 points trdeg = 1 = dim.

sources.match: Proves the equivalence of being weakly Shilov, the transcendence degree of the secondary residue field equalling the local dimension (via Poineau, Lemme 4.4 and Corollaire 4.15), and specialising to a generic point of the special fibre of a formal model (via Raynaud, Bosch's Lectures Theorem 8.4.3).

sources.locator: §4, Lemma 4.4, p. 284; Corollaries 4.15 and 4.18, pp. 287–288; Remark 4.14(ii), p. 287

nodes.title: Weakly Shilov points avoid nowhere dense Zariski closed sets
nodes.statement: Let X be a rigid space over K and Z ⊆ X a nowhere dense Zariski closed subset. Then Z contains no weakly Shilov point of X. Consequently: (i) if X is reduced, every weakly Shilov point lies in the regular locus Reg(X); (ii) if X is irreducible and Z ⊊ X is Zariski closed, Z contains no weakly Shilov point; (iii) a subset of |X| that contains all weakly Shilov points, or whose complement is a countable union of nowhere dense Zariski closed sets, is dense.
hypotheses: For (ii), proper Zariski closed subsets of irreducible spaces are nowhere dense (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.1/irreducibility-criterion).
proofSteps: If z ∈ Z is weakly Shilov in X, then trdeg K̃_z = dim_z X (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.4/weakly-shilov-transcendence-criterion); but z is also a rank-one point of Z with the same completed residue field, so trdeg K̃_z ≤ dim_z Z (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.4/abhyankar-bound) < dim_z X (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.0/nowhere-dense-criteria(e)). Contradiction.
(i): Sing(X) is a nowhere dense Zariski closed subset when X is reduced (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.2/singular-locus).

nodes.title: Blow-up sequences and their flat pullbacks
nodes.statement: Let X be a locally noetherian scheme. A blow-up of X is the blow-up Bl_V(X) → X along a fixed closed subscheme V (the centre is part of the data); it is empty if V = ∅. A blow-up sequence of length n is a chain X_n → ⋯ → X_1 → X_0 = X with X_{i+1} = Bl_{V_i}(X_i); it is contracted if no blow-up is empty, and a trivial extension of a sequence is obtained by inserting empty blow-ups. For a flat g : Y → X the pullback g^*(X_n ⇢ X) is the sequence Y ×_X X_i with centres Y ×_X V_i, again a blow-up sequence. A sequence is T-supported if its centres lie over T, and strong if its centres are regular. The same definitions apply to rigid spaces with the rigid blow-ups of AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.5/rigid-blow-up and flat morphisms of rigid spaces.
hypotheses: Blow-ups of schemes along closed subschemes (Rees algebra, universal property that the preimage of V is an effective Cartier divisor) are those of AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry R09.7a, there for varieties, here for locally noetherian schemes; the construction is the same.
An empty blow-up in Temkin’s sequence convention means the identity stage with empty centre (unit ideal); it does not mean the blow-up of the zero ideal, whose total space is empty.
proofSteps: Blow-ups commute with flat base change: Bl_{V ×_X Y}(Y) = Y ×_X Bl_V(X) for Y → X flat (Temkin §2.2.5), so pullbacks of sequences are sequences.
Equality of sequences is isomorphism compatible with centres; it is unique when it exists (Temkin §2.2.3).
Pushforward along pro-open immersions by schematic closure of centres (Temkin Lemma 2.2.1).
acceptance: The blow-up of A² at the origin is a contracted sequence of length 1 whose pullback to A² − {0} is an empty blow-up.
A blow-up along a Cartier divisor is an isomorphism of schemes but a non-empty blow-up in a sequence.

nodes.title: Blow-ups of rigid spaces along coherent ideals
nodes.statement: Let X be a rigid space over K and 𝓘 ⊆ O_X a coherent ideal. The blow-up π : Bl_𝓘(X) → X is the relative analytification of Proj_X(⊕_{n≥0} 𝓘^n): over an affinoid open U = Spa(A, A°) with 𝓘|_U = Ĩ it is (Proj ⊕ I^n)^an relative to Spa(A, A°), and these glue. π is proper, 𝓘·O_{Bl} is an invertible ideal, π is an isomorphism over X − V(𝓘), and π is universal among morphisms Y → X with 𝓘·O_Y invertible. Formation commutes with flat base change Y → X (in particular with restriction to opens and with smooth morphisms). If X is reduced and V(𝓘) is nowhere dense, π^{-1}(V(𝓘)) is a nowhere dense Cartier divisor and Bl_𝓘(X) is reduced.
hypotheses: Relative analytification over Spec A is AdicSpacesPartII:R1/scheme-fibre-product-analytification. Projective-space properness is AdicSpacesPartII:R1/analytic-projective-space-proper; apply it relatively over the affinoid base.

Use relative analytification over Spec A for the blow-up of an affinoid ideal. For the birational and nowhere-dense-exceptional assertions assume the centre is nowhere dense; a zero ideal gives empty Proj and is not a surjective modification.
proofSteps: Affinoid chart: P = Proj ⊕ I^n is projective over Spec A; its relative analytification over Spa(A, A°) is proper (AdicSpacesPartII:R1/analytic-projective-space-proper and closed immersions).
Gluing: for an affinoid subdomain A → A′ (flat), Proj ⊕ (IA′)^n = P ×_{Spec A} Spec A′ and relative analytification commutes with this base change, so the charts glue.
Universal property: on each chart it is the analytification of the universal property of the algebraic blow-up, via the universal property of relative analytification.
Flat base change: the Rees algebra of 𝓘 commutes with flat pullback.
Nowhere density of the exceptional divisor: on a reduced X with V(𝓘) nowhere dense, π is an isomorphism over the dense Zariski open X − V(𝓘) and π^{-1}(V(𝓘)) is cut out locally by one nonzerodivisor.
acceptance: The blow-up of the 2-dimensional polydisc at the origin has exceptional divisor the analytified P¹_K; the blow-up of the disc at the origin is an isomorphism.

nodes.title: Functorial desingularization of varieties in characteristic zero
nodes.statement: There is a rule F_Var assigning to every generically reduced scheme X of finite type over a field of characteristic 0 (and to finite disjoint unions of such) a contracted strong blow-up sequence F_Var(X) : X_n ⇢ X with regular X_n and centres disjoint from the preimages of the regular locus, such that for every regular morphism g : X′ → X in this category, F_Var(X′) is the contraction of g^*F_Var(X). The set of its invariants is countable.
hypotheses: Regular morphisms: flat with geometrically regular fibres (SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.0/regular-algebra-map); between varieties over the same field these include all smooth morphisms; base field extensions are regular in characteristic 0.
proofSteps: The Bierstone–Milman algorithm (AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry:R09.7/embedded-resolution and R09.7/local-isomorphism-resolution) gives a strong desingularization of reduced varieties compatible with local isomorphisms.
Compatibility with smooth morphisms (Bierstone–Milman, Functoriality in resolution of singularities, 2008): the local invariant is unchanged under smooth morphisms, so the centres pull back.

Compatibility with all regular morphisms and with disjoint unions over different fields (Bierstone–Milman–Temkin, Q-universal desingularization, 2011): every regular morphism of varieties is a limit of smooth morphisms; the algorithm is induced from its restriction to varieties over Q.
Countability of invariants: every variety admits a regular morphism to a variety over Q, and there are countably many of those up to isomorphism (Temkin Remark 2.3.6).
acceptance: For the cuspidal curve y² = x³ over Q the sequence is a single blow-up of the origin; its pullback to the cusp over any field of characteristic 0 is its sequence.

sources.match: Defines desingularization, strong and functorial desingularization, gluing from affine pieces through disjoint unions, and states the functorial strong desingularization of characteristic-zero varieties with respect to regular morphisms, citing Bierstone–Milman and Bierstone–Milman–Temkin.

nodes.title: Temkin's functorial desingularization of quasi-excellent schemes over Q
nodes.statement: For every noetherian quasi-excellent generically reduced scheme X over Spec Q there is a blow-up sequence F(X) : X_n ⇢ X_0 = X such that (i) its centres are disjoint from the preimages of the regular locus X_reg, (ii) its centres are regular, (iii) X_n is regular, and (iv) F is functorial for all regular morphisms X′ → X: F(X′) is obtained from F(X) ×_X X′ by omitting the empty blow-ups. For arbitrary nonreduced noetherian quasi-excellent X over Q, Remark 1.2.2 also gives a functorial construction for regular maps, but it may delete generically nonreduced components and need not be surjective. This extension is not the resolution used for diamond covers.
hypotheses: Quasi-excellent schemes and regular morphisms as in SchemeAndStackFoundations SF.0; generically reduced means the non-reduced locus is nowhere dense.
proofSteps: Black-box strategy (Temkin §1.3): extend F_Var (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.5/functorial-desingularization-varieties) first to formal varieties and to schemes whose singular locus is small (§3), using Elkik–Gabber–Ramero type algebraization of the formal neighbourhood of the singular locus (Theorem 3.2.3) and the intrinsic dependence of the desingularization on the formal completion along the singular locus (§3.3, Theorem 3.4.1).

Induction on the codimension of the singular locus (§4.1): resolve generically along the singular locus, then extend over the closure by pushforward along pro-open immersions (Temkin Lemma 2.2.1), synchronised by disjoint unions (Lemma 2.3.3).

The main construction §4.3 assembles a compatible sequence of these partial resolutions and proves functoriality for regular morphisms; quasi-excellence enters through Nishimura–Nishimura's theorem on completions (Theorem 2.1.6) or Gabber's (Theorem 2.1.8).

For general X, first resolve X_red and push the blow-ups forward to X. The resulting space X′ has regular reduction. Blow up the reduction of its generically nonreduced components, obtaining a generically reduced X′′, then apply F(X′′). This final application is required. The full construction is functorial for regular maps (Temkin Remark 1.2.2(i)).
acceptance: A regular X has F(X) = the empty sequence; for X the spectrum of the cusp k⟦x, y⟧/(y² − x³) the sequence blows up the closed point once.

nodes.title: Functorial resolution of singularities of rigid spaces
nodes.statement: Let K have characteristic 0 and X be a rigid space over K whose non-reduced locus is nowhere dense (for instance X reduced). There is a countable blow-up hypersequence of rigid blow-ups with regular (smooth) centres, locally finite over X and stabilising over every quasi-compact open, with limit π : X_∞ → X, such that X_∞ is smooth over K, every centre lies over Sing(X) and is disjoint from the preimage of Reg(X), and π is a proper morphism which is an isomorphism over Reg(X) = X^sm. The construction is functorial for smooth morphisms X′ → X (the hypersequence of X′ is the pullback with empty blow-ups removed) and compatible with complete extensions of K. For quasi-compact X the hypersequence is a finite blow-up sequence.
hypotheses: Rigid spaces in Temkin's sense (Tate's), here read through Huber's functor on quasi-separated spaces and glued on general ones; regular morphisms in the rigid category are smooth morphisms.
Nowhere dense non-reduced locus: Temkin's category C. For arbitrary X apply the theorem to X_red (see AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.5/resolution-consequences).
proofSteps: Quasi-compact case (Temkin Theorem 5.2.2): cover X by finitely many affinoids X_i = Spa(A_i) and the pairwise intersections by affinoids X_ijk; A_i, A_ijk are excellent and A_i → A_ijk are regular (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.0/affinoid-localization-regular).

Apply F (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.5/functorial-desingularization-qe) to Spec A_i (generically reduced, quasi-excellent) and analytify the centres to get rigid blow-up sequences of the X_i (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.5/rigid-blow-up); by functoriality for the regular maps A_i → A_ijk they agree on overlaps and glue, disjoint unions synchronising the order of blow-ups (Temkin Lemmas 2.3.1, 2.3.3).

Regularity transfers: X_n is regular at classical points iff the algebraic X_n is regular at closed points (same completions), and regular = smooth in characteristic 0 (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.2/smooth-iff-regular).

Non-compact case (Temkin Theorem 5.3.2): saturate with empty blow-ups indexed by the countable set of invariants; the hypersequences of the affinoid charts agree on overlaps and glue to a countable blow-up hypersequence whose limit X_∞ → X is a single proper morphism.
Functoriality for smooth X′ → X: affinoid charts of X′ map by smooth, hence regular, ring maps to those of X (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.0/affinoid-localization-regular).

Ground-field-extension compatibility is a separate assertion of Temkin Theorem 5.2.2, p. 33. A derivation from the scheme functor requires regularity of the completed affinoid scalar-extension map in characteristic zero; flatness alone does not suffice. G3 records this proof input.
acceptance: The resolution of the cuspidal disc is its normalization by one blow-up of the cusp; the resolution of a smooth space is the identity.

nodes.title: Properties of the resolution used by Howe–Klevdal
nodes.statement: Let L be a complete nonarchimedean field over Q_p and S a reduced rigid space over L with resolution π : S̃ → S (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.5/rigid-resolution). Then: (i) π is proper and surjective, S̃ is smooth, and π restricts to an isomorphism π^{-1}(S^sm) ≅ S^sm onto the dense Zariski open S^sm, with π^{-1}(S^sm) dense Zariski open in S̃; (ii) π^♢ : S̃^♢ → S^♢ is a surjection of v-sheaves (a v-cover); (iii) for every rigid space T, T^♢ = (T_red)^♢, so T_red's resolution serves for T, for instance for T = S̃ ×_S S̃, and (S̃ ×_S S̃)^♢ = S̃^♢ ×_{S^♢} S̃^♢; (iv) if S is irreducible then S̃ is connected (and irreducible).
hypotheses: S reduced, so its non-reduced locus is empty and Temkin's theorem applies; L of characteristic 0 (over Q_p).
proofSteps: (i) Surjectivity: π is an isomorphism over the dense S^sm (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.2/smooth-iff-regular, RZ.2/singular-locus) and proper, so its image is closed (Zariski closed, AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.0/proper-image-zariski-closed) and contains a dense set, hence is everything. Density of π^{-1}(S^sm): its complement is contained in the union of the exceptional divisors, nowhere dense Cartier divisors (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.5/rigid-blow-up).

(ii) |S̃^♢| → |S^♢| is |π|, surjective (DiamondsAndVStacks:D6/etale-site-comparison), and π^♢ is quasi-compact because π is; a quasi-compact map of v-sheaves surjective on spaces is a v-surjection (DiamondsAndVStacks:D4/spaces-and-surjectivity-for-small-v-stacks).

(iii) A map from a perfectoid space to T factors uniquely through T_red because perfectoid spaces are uniform (reduced); fibre products of rigid spaces go to fibre products of diamonds (DiamondsAndVStacks:D6/gluing-and-the-diamond-functor).

(iv) S irreducible ⇒ S^sm ≅ π^{-1}(S^sm) is a dense Zariski open of S, hence irreducible and connected (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.1/dense-open-connected); it is dense in |S̃| by (i), and the closure of a connected set is connected; S̃ smooth and connected is irreducible.
acceptance: For S the cuspidal disc, S̃ is the disc, π is bijective, and π^♢ is an isomorphism because S^♢ only sees the seminormalization.
For S = Spa(K⟨X,Y⟩/(XY)) (reducible), S̃ is two discs: not connected, as (iv) allows.

nodes.title: The analytic inverse function theorem over complete fields
nodes.statement: Let F be a complete nontrivially normed field, E, E′ finite-dimensional normed F-spaces, U ⊆ E open and f : U → E′ analytic (locally given by convergent power series) with df_a : E → E′ bijective at a ∈ U. Then there are open neighbourhoods W ∋ a and W′ ∋ f(a) such that f restricts to a homeomorphism W → W′ whose inverse is analytic. If f is given on the polydisc of radius ε by power series with coefficients in F, the inverse is given by power series on a polydisc of explicit radius δ (Schneider Proposition 5.9). The same holds for analytic maps of F-analytic manifolds (Schneider Proposition 9.3).
hypotheses: F need not be locally compact or of characteristic 0; analytic means AnalyticAt at every point (Mathlib), which for F nonarchimedean is Schneider's 'locally analytic'.
proofSteps: An analytic map has a strict derivative (Mathlib AnalyticAt.hasStrictFDerivAt); since E is complete and df_a invertible, HasStrictFDerivAt.toOpenPartialHomeomorph gives a local homeomorphism.

Its inverse has a power series expansion at f(a) given by the left inverse of the power series of f (Mathlib OpenPartialHomeomorph.hasFPowerSeriesAt_symm); applying this at every point of W gives analyticity of the inverse on W′.
Manifold version: compose with charts (Schneider Proposition 9.3).
acceptance: f(x) = x + x² on Q_p is an analytic isomorphism near 0 with inverse given by a power series converging on |y| < 1.
f(x) = x^p on Z_p has df_0 = 0; it is not a local isomorphism at 0.

sources.match: For a power series f in r variables over a complete nonarchimedean field with f(0) = 0 and bijective derivative at 0, there is a unique power series inverse on an explicitly smaller polydisc.

nodes.title: The constant rank theorem for analytic maps
nodes.statement: Let F be a complete nontrivially normed field of characteristic 0, M and N analytic manifolds over F of dimensions m and n (Mathlib ChartedSpace with IsManifold over the model space F^m, smoothness ω), and f : M → N an analytic map such that the rank of the tangent map T_x f is equal to k for all x in a neighbourhood of a. Then there are analytic charts φ around a and ψ around f(a) such that ψ ∘ f ∘ φ^{-1}(x_1, …, x_m) = (x_1, …, x_k, 0, …, 0) near φ(a). In particular f is locally a submersion onto a k-dimensional submanifold; if k = n, f is open near a.
hypotheses: Constant rank on a neighbourhood is essential; maximal rank at a point gives it on a neighbourhood only when the rank is m or n.
Characteristic 0 is essential: in characteristic p the map x ↦ x^p has constant rank 0 without being locally constant.

For rigid-space applications F is nonarchimedean. The suggested model-space statement uses Mathlib’s general complete nontrivially normed field; its coordinate proof uses the existing analytic inverse theorem and uniqueness of convergent power series. Serre is a secondary locator in HK2, not an independently inspected source.
proofSteps: Reduce to model spaces: f : U ⊆ F^m → F^n analytic, a = 0, f(0) = 0, df_0 of rank k; after linear changes of coordinates df_0 = [I_k 0; 0 0].

Put g(x) = (f_1(x), …, f_k(x), x_{k+1}, …, x_m); dg_0 is invertible, so g is a local analytic isomorphism (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.6/analytic-inverse-function-theorem), and f ∘ g^{-1}(y) = (y_1, …, y_k, h(y)).

Constant rank k forces ∂h/∂y_j = 0 for j > k near 0, so h depends only on (y_1, …, y_k) on a polydisc (in characteristic 0, a power series whose partial derivatives in y_{k+1}, …, y_m vanish on a polydisc does not involve those variables, by the identity theorem for power series, Schneider Corollary 5.8).
Then ψ(z) = (z_1, …, z_k, z_{k+1} − h_{k+1}(z_1, …, z_k), …) is a local analytic isomorphism of F^n with ψ ∘ f ∘ g^{-1} = (y_1, …, y_k, 0, …, 0).
This is Serre's theorem on subimmersions (Lie algebras and Lie groups, Part II, Chapter III), cited by Howe–Klevdal; Serre was not read here.
acceptance: f(x, y) = (x, 0) on F² has constant rank 1 and is already in normal form; f(x) = x² on F has rank 1 off 0 and rank 0 at 0, so the theorem applies on F − {0} but not at 0.
Over a field of characteristic p the conclusion fails for x ↦ x^p, which has constant rank 0.

sources.match: Applies the constant rank theorem (Serre, Lie algebras and Lie groups, theorem on subimmersions, p. 86) to f_C : V(C) → Fl(C) to find charts in which f_C is a coordinate projection followed by inclusion.

sources.locator: §5, Corollary 5.8 and Proposition 5.9, p. 33; §9, Proposition 9.3, p. 58

nodes.title: Polydisc neighbourhoods of rational points of smooth rigid spaces
nodes.statement: Let F be a complete nontrivially nonarchimedean normed field and V a rigid space over F, smooth of dimension m at an F-rational point x. Then x has a basis of open neighbourhoods in |V| each isomorphic, as a rigid space, to a closed polydisc of dimension m and radius in |F^×|, centred at x. More generally, a morphism f : V → W of smooth rigid spaces with df_x bijective at an F-rational x restricts to an isomorphism of polydisc neighbourhoods of x and f(x).
hypotheses: x is F-rational: k(x) = F. For non-rational classical points pass to V_{k(x)}.
F is nonarchimedean. Polydisc neighbourhood means an admissible open isomorphic to a closed polydisc; its embedding in the original ambient coordinates need not be a standard round disc.
proofSteps: Near x, V is étale over a polydisc (AdicSpacesPartII:R0/smooth-local-structure); locally V is a closed subspace of a polydisc D^{m+r} cut out by r functions h_1, …, h_r whose differentials together with dT_1, …, dT_m form a basis (AdicSpacesPartII:R0/jacobian-criterion-closed-subspace).

Apply the convergent power-series inverse theorem to (T,h) at the rational point. Choose a target closed polydisc strictly inside the convergence neighbourhood of the inverse series. The inverse series and the original map then define inverse rigid morphisms between this target and its image neighbourhood. This image is an affinoid open isomorphic to a polydisc, but need not be a standard-radius ambient polydisc.

In these coordinates V is {h = 0} = the polydisc of radius δ in the first m coordinates; shrinking δ gives the basis (polydiscs of radii |c|^k form a neighbourhood basis of the rational point 0, AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.3/polydisc-points-topology).
The relative statement follows by applying this to the graph of f.
acceptance: For V = G_m^an and x = 1, the discs {|T − 1| ≤ |c|} are neighbourhoods isomorphic to closed discs; for the cusp at the origin no neighbourhood is a disc (not smooth there).

nodes.title: The analytic manifold of rational points of a smooth rigid space
nodes.statement: Let F be a complete nontrivially nonarchimedean normed field and V a rigid space over F, smooth of pure dimension m. The set V(F) of F-rational points, with the subspace topology from |V|, carries a unique structure of F-analytic manifold of dimension m (Mathlib ChartedSpace (Fin m → F) with IsManifold 𝓘(F, Fin m → F) ω) whose charts are the coordinate maps of the polydisc neighbourhoods of AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.6/rigid-inverse-function-theorem. A morphism f : V → W of smooth rigid spaces induces an analytic map f_F : V(F) → W(F) with tangent map T_x f_F = df_x on Zariski tangent spaces (T_x(V(F)) = T_x V). For E a complete field, V smooth over E and E′/E a finite extension or a complete algebraically closed extension (such as the completion C of an algebraic closure), V(E′) := V_{E′}(E′) is an E′-analytic manifold of dimension m; for E′ = E finite over Q_p this is Serre's p-adic manifold.
hypotheses: Pure dimension m; for V of varying dimension the construction is done on each connected component.

Mathlib IsManifold does not imply Hausdorffness or second countability. If V is separated then V(F) is Hausdorff and fits Schneider’s convention; no global Hausdorff claim is made for a general smooth nonseparated V.
proofSteps: Charts: polydisc neighbourhoods U ≅ D^m(δ) of rational points give bijections U(F) ≅ (radius-δ ball in F^m), homeomorphisms by AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.3/polydisc-points-topology.
Transition maps between two such charts are given by restricted power series, hence analytic (Mathlib AnalyticOnNhd); so the atlas is in the analytic groupoid.
Morphisms: in charts f is given by power series, so f_F is analytic; its derivative at x is the Jacobian, i.e. df_x (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.2/tangent-space).
Uniqueness: any two atlases built from polydisc neighbourhoods are compatible by the same argument.
Base change to E′ uses V_{E′} = V ×_E Spa E′ (smooth of the same dimension, AdicSpacesPartII:R0/smooth-etale-base-change).
acceptance: V = D^1 over Q_p: V(Q_p) = Z_p as an open subset of Q_p; V = G_m^an: V(F) = F^× with its analytic structure.

nodes.title: Smooth morphisms give submersions; orbit maps are submersions
nodes.statement: Let F be a complete nontrivially nonarchimedean normed field of characteristic 0 and f : V → W a smooth morphism of smooth rigid spaces over F. Then f_F : V(F) → W(F) is a submersion: T_x f_F is surjective for all x ∈ V(F), so f_F is open and locally a projection in charts. In particular, if G is a smooth linear algebraic group over a subfield E ⊆ F, H ⊆ G a closed subgroup and y ∈ (G/H)(F), the orbit map G(F) → (G/H)(F), g ↦ g·y, is a submersion at every point.
hypotheses: Smoothness of the quotient map G → G/H for a smooth closed subgroup H in characteristic 0 (H is smooth by Cartier's theorem) comes from the Tau Ceti roadmap ReductiveGroups, Layer 3 (quotients G/H as fppf sheaves, representable, with G → G/H an H-torsor).
proofSteps: Smooth f: df_x is surjective at rational x by the differential criterion (AdicSpacesPartII:R0/differential-criterion-morphism: f^*Ω_W → Ω_V split injective near x), so T_x f_F = df_x is surjective (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.6/manifold-of-classical-points).
Constant rank n = dim W on V(F), so the constant rank theorem gives a projection in charts (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.6/constant-rank-theorem).

For y ∈ (G/H)(F), choose a faithfully flat field extension F′/F over which y lifts to g_0 ∈ G(F′). After this extension the algebraic orbit morphism is the quotient G_{F′} → (G/H)_{F′} composed with right translation by g_0. In characteristic zero H is smooth, so this is a smooth H-torsor. Smoothness descends to F; analytify and apply the first part. Surjectivity on F-points of G → G/H is not assumed.
acceptance: For G = GL_2 acting on P¹ = GL_2/B, the orbit map of ∞ is a submersion GL_2(F) → P¹(F).

nodes.title: Identity theorem across a closed subfield
nodes.statement: Let E ⊆ C be complete nontrivially normed fields of characteristic 0 with E closed in C and the norm on E the restriction of that of C. If φ is analytic on a neighbourhood of 0 in C^m and vanishes on a neighbourhood of 0 in E^m, then φ vanishes on a neighbourhood of 0 in C^m. Consequently, if G is a smooth algebraic group over E, K_0 ≤ G(E) an open subgroup and φ an analytic function on a neighbourhood of 1 in G(C) vanishing on K_0, then φ vanishes on a neighbourhood of 1 in G(C).
hypotheses: Characteristic 0 for Schneider's identity theorem (Corollary 5.8); it holds without that hypothesis by Bosch–Güntzer–Remmert 5.1.4, not used here.
proofSteps: Expand φ(z) = Σ_α c_α z^α with c_α ∈ C on a polydisc of radius ε ∈ |E^×|. Its restriction to E^m is a power series in m variables over E with coefficients in the E-Banach space C, converging on the E-polydisc of radius ε.

That restriction vanishes on a neighbourhood of 0, hence (Schneider, Corollary 5.8, applied to power series with values in an E-Banach space, after rescaling to the neighbourhood) all c_α = 0, so φ = 0 near 0 in C^m.

For G: choose a chart of G(E) at 1 coming from a polydisc neighbourhood of 1 in G^an defined over E (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.6/rigid-inverse-function-theorem); after base change it is a chart of G(C) at 1 (AdicSpacesPartIIPartII:RZ.6/manifold-of-classical-points, compatibility with base change) in which G(E) near 1 is E^m ∩ (ball) ⊆ C^m and K_0 contains an E-ball.
acceptance: For E = Q_p, C = C_p and m = 1, a power series Σ c_n z^n with c_n ∈ C_p that vanishes on p^k Z_p has all c_n = 0.
z ↦ z(z − a) with a ∈ C − E vanishes at the E-point 0 but on no E-neighbourhood of 0: vanishing on an open set of E-points is needed.
